meta.title: Agile Earth Observation Satellite Scheduling with Hybrid Repair and Pointer-Based Reinforcement Learning
meta.authorsHtml: F. Favaretto<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, S. Giannattasio<sup>2</sup>, G. Volpi<sup>3</sup>, L. Petronzio<sup>4</sup>

abstract: Agile Earth observation (EO) satellites must select imaging and downlink opportunities in real time while respecting attitude agility, energy, storage, and payload-duty constraints. We couple an Orekit-based physics simulator with a deterministic repair routine and a proximal policy optimization (PPO) agent that proposes incremental edits to a warmstarted, ground-uplinked plan. Each decision is a scalar index into a fixed-capacity but dynamically populated bank of imaging, downlink, reinsertion, charging, and Noop actions. The repair routine commits feasible insertions and may evict lowerpriority imaging activities; removed activities with remaining visibility windows are exposed for reinsertion. We compare two MLP policies with a pointer-based Transformer that preserves the typed candidate structure. Across 1000 held-out episodes per policy, paired by seed, the pointer policy achieves higher mean return (64.3 versus 51.0 and 42.3), executes about 2.5 times more successful downlinks, and proposes fewer infeasible actions. This gain is accompanied by greater plan churn; some unreinserted activities can arise from fixed-window warm-start tasks that cannot be rescheduled after eviction. The results support candidate-wise attention as a useful inductive bias for hybrid on-board replanning, while exposing the operational trade-off between accumulated utility and schedule stability.

blocks.html: Agile Earth observation (EO) satellites can rapidly slew to image diverse targets, enabling high-value services such as disaster response, maritime monitoring, and time-critical intelligence. The same agility also makes planning harder: imaging windows are short, attitude maneuvers couple consecutive tasks, and battery, storage, payload duty, and sparse downlink contacts create dependencies across the planning horizon. Mixed-integer formulations and heuristic or metaheuristic schedulers can produce strong offline plans, but repeated optimization becomes difficult when requests, resource levels, and the executable timeline change on board.

Over the last two decades, agile EO scheduling has been addressed with exact mixed-integer and constraint-based formulations, constructive and repair heuristics, and metaheuristics; surveys summarize this evolution and its open challenges [1]. Exact formulations can certify optimality on small instances, but their cost grows rapidly with the number of candidate windows and operational constraints [2]. Deep reinforcement learning offers a complementary approach by amortizing computation across procedurally generated instances: graph and attention policies trained with PPO can construct schedules quickly at execution time [3–5]. In parallel, the Basilisk ecosystem has supported learning-based on-board planning studies with realistic spacecraft dynamics and scalable training workflows [5–7].

This work studies single-satellite agile EO replanning with realistic orbital geometry and coupled resources. A learned policy does not replace the scheduler: it selects the next candidate-level edit, while a deterministic repair layer verifies geometry and resources, resolves local conflicts, and maintains a feasible timeline. This separation gives the policy informative failure signals while keeping hard operational logic outside the neural network. The evaluation compares policy architectures under the same procedural scenario distribution and warm-start mechanism. A pointer-based policy achieves the highest test return, mainly through stronger downlink use and better feasibility awareness, but also modifies the initial plan more aggressively.
Contributions. We present:
• a physics-aware, Gymnasium-compatible testbed that combines Orekit access computation, battery, storage, payload-duty, and ground-contact models with a procedurally generated warm-start plan [8];

• a hybrid replanning loop in which a learned policy selects incremental edits and a deterministic repair routine inserts them, evicts only lower-priority imaging activities when necessary, and exposes reschedulable removals as reinsertion candidates;
• a controlled comparison of a typed-candidate Pointer Transformer and two MLP PPO baselines
over 1000 paired held-out episodes, including return, feasibility, downlink, Noop, repair, training, and computational-footprint diagnostics.

We study a single low Earth orbit satellite over a sixhour horizon. Orekit propagation provides time-tagged target visibility, ground-station contacts, eclipse state, and attitude geometry. Each episode starts from a warm-start plan: a procedurally generated sequence of imaging and downlink activities that represents a timeline previously prepared by the ground segment. At decision time tk, the policy selects an incremental edit. The deterministic repair routine first searches for a feasible execution time inside the selected window. When direct insertion fails because of overlap or payload-duty saturation, only lower-priority imaging activities are eligible for eviction. Feasible repair alternatives are ordered by the number of removals and then by lost priority, so the routine prefers the least disruptive valid edit. Removed activities with usable episode visibility windows enter a reinsertion set. Synthetic warm-start activities carry priorities but no visibility catalogue; consequently, once evicted they cannot be reinserted.

There is no finite library of baseline scenarios. Every reset samples a new target catalogue and priorities, visibility windows on a precomputed orbital rail, initial storage and battery state, payload-duty condition, and warm-start timeline. The total target population is sampled from {60, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 600}, while only the ten currently selected imaging candidates are exposed to the policy. Each model was trained for 40 million environment steps, corresponding to approximately 344,000 procedurally generated episodes per policy; evaluation uses a separate set of 1000 paired seeds. Target identities are not encoded. Therefore, a trained checkpoint can accept previously unseen targets and updated requests when they use the same action types, normalized feature schema, resource semantics, and configured slot capacities. Transfer to substantially different spacecraft dynamics, constraints, or action classes was not evaluated and would normally require adaptation or retraining.

The repair routine evaluates candidate insertions with a constraint engine that combines geometry checks with three coupled resource models. Storage has capacity Smax; imaging occupies slots and downlinking frees them at the configured rate. Battery energy E(t) has capacity Emax, is depleted by the continuous spacecraft load and additional imaging or downlink loads, and is replenished by passive solar input and optional charging actions. Payload duty limits accumulated imaging exposure within each orbit to a fraction α of the orbital period. The timeline representation also includes the pre- and post-imaging slew intervals used by the conflict and geometry checks.

Actions. The action is a scalar discrete index, not a variable-length vector. The fixed-capacity interface is summarized in Table 1: ten outputs address imaging candidates, two address ground-station downlinks, two address reinsertion candidates, and the final two represent charging and Noop. The candidate contents change as windows expire, new objectives become current, or removed tasks become eligible for reinsertion; unused positions are padded. Consequently, a new imaging request is encoded by placing its window and features in an imaging slot, without changing the output dimension. A new objective type, or a candidate population exceeding the configured capacity, would require an interface change. No feasibility mask removes geometrically or resource-infeasible candidates. The Pointer Transformer masks only absent padded candidates; an infeasible proposal is still passed to repair and penalized.

Observations. All policies receive the same 221 normalized values, (1) 11 + 10×16 + 2×16 + 2×9 = 221, with the block layout in Table 1. Global features summarize time, free-time and congestion information, sunlight, storage, payload duty, orbit progress, and battery state. Candidate blocks encode priority, timing, illumination, local fit and overlap descriptors, resource pressure, and predicted battery state. Missing blocks are filled with −1. The MLP baselines consume the resulting vector directly. The Transformer uses exactly the same information but reconstructs one global token, ten imaging tokens, two reinsertion tokens, and two ground-station tokens, and prepends a learned context token.

blocks.html: The imaging eviction term is clipped at 1.2, so a successful image cannot become negative solely because of repair. The living term weakly discourages delay, while battery depletion terminates the episode with the indicated penalty.

We compare PPO [9] with two independent policy/value MLPs, using hidden dimensions [256, 256] and [512, 256], against the Pointer Transformer in Figure 1. For the latter, type-specific MLP encoders map the global, imaging, reinsertion, and ground-station blocks to width d = 128. Learned type and position embeddings are added before a one-layer, four-head Transformer encoder with GELU feed-forward width 4d and no dropout. A learned context token is refined by cross-attention over the encoded candidates, and a type-specific MLP scorer with hidden width 256 produces candidate logits; charging and Noop use separate heads. Because candidate slots are time ordered and use learned position embeddings, the network is not strictly permutation invariant; its relevant inductive bias is candidate-wise attention and typed scoring rather than flattening all blocks before action selection.

All policies use learning rate 5×10−5, γ = 0.99, GAE with λ = 0.75, clip parameter 0.2, gradient clipping at 1.0, batches of 80,000 samples, minibatches of 256, and three epochs per iteration. The entropy coefficient steps. Training used 55 environment runners on a virtual machine with 64 CPU cores, 64 GB RAM, and a 24 GB NVIDIA H100 MIG partition.

blocks.html: Table 2 consolidates model size, total training time, and the archived rollout timers. The environment-step timer includes action routing, deterministic repair, resource advancement, and construction of the next observation. These host-side measurements indicate the order of magnitude of the implemented control loop, but they are not benchmarks on flight-qualified hardware.

Figure 2 reports the composite PPO loss and mean episodic return over 40 million environment steps. The logged total loss combines the clipped policy surrogate, value-function fitting, entropy regularization, and the adaptive KL contribution. All three losses settle to a similar range, but this does not imply equivalent policies: the component scales depend on advantage normalization and value fitting, whereas episodic return measures scheduling performance directly. The return curves separate during training and retain the ordering observed in held-out evaluation, with the Pointer Transformer reaching the highest level.

blocks.html: Each checkpoint is evaluated on 1000 held-out episodes using identical episode seeds across policies and deterministic action selection, enabling paired comparisons. We report episodic return, successful imaging and downlink actions, infeasible-action rate, Noop behavior, and repair diagnostics. The evaluation is designed to answer which learned selector most effectively drives the same deterministic repair mechanism from the same operational prior. Accordingly, the procedurally generated warm-start plan is a common initial condition, not a fourth scheduling policy. The saved evaluation does not separately score that plan without any agent edits, so we make no numerical claim against a frozen ground schedule. This scope does not affect the fairness of the architecture comparison: all three policies receive identical initial scenarios and are compared episode by episode.

The Pointer Transformer achieves mean return 64.33 ± 41.62, compared with 50.95 ± 36.66 for MLP512 and 42.30 ± 39.28 for MLP256 (Table 3 and Figure 3). In paired episode-wise comparisons, it outperforms MLP256 in 80.6% of episodes, with mean paired advantage 22.0, and MLP512 in 74.1%, with advantage 13.4. Across all three policies, it attains the highest return in 70.8% of episodes.

The return gain is associated most clearly with downlink use and feasibility awareness (Table 3 and Figure 3). The Pointer Transformer completes 6.01 successful downlinks per episode, versus 2.44 and 2.26 for the MLPs, reducing storage pressure and supporting more successful imaging. It also has the lowest infeasible-action rate, 3.14% versus 4.83% and 6.23%, indicating that it learns the acceptance boundary of the deterministic repair layer more accurately.

blocks.html: The corresponding trade-off is greater plan churn (Table 4). Lower-priority warm-start imaging activities may be removed to admit a higher-priority candidate. Because those synthetic activities have no associated visibility windows, they cannot subsequently appear in the reinsertion bank. The evaluation files do not label unreinserted tasks by origin, so the higher Transformer count cannot be decomposed exactly; nevertheless, fixed-window warm-start removals provide a direct mechanism for part of the difference. The result should therefore be interpreted as a more aggressive policy–repair operating point, rather than as evidence that the repair routine itself fails to seek reinsertion.

The results support candidate-wise attention as a strong inductive bias for agile EO replanning. Although all policies use the same fixed 16-output interface and the same 221 observation values, the Pointer Transformer preserves the block structure of the changing candidate bank instead of requiring early flattening. It wins most paired episodes, exploits downlink opportunities more consistently, and proposes fewer actions rejected by repair. In this resource regime, downlink quality has a cascading effect: relieving storage pressure preserves the ability to accept later imaging opportunities.

The deterministic repair layer is not merely a safety filter. Its success and failure outcomes define the effective feasibility boundary learned by the policy, and its eviction rule permits a high-priority opportunity to replace lower-priority imaging activities. The Transformer uses that option more often. Since synthetic warm-start tasks have no alternative visibility windows, some evictions necessarily remain unreinserted; however, the current logger does not distinguish warm-start from ordinary removed tasks, so the exact share cannot be quantified from the saved evaluation. More generally, the observed aggressiveness is a joint effect of architecture, reward shaping, and the repair rule. Similar PPO losses across models only show that the composite optimization objectives stabilized; they do not contradict the clear differences in episodic return and behavior.

blocks.html: The MLPs occupy a more conservative operating point. MLP<sup>256</sup> has the highest Noop rate and leaves more feasible opportunities unused, whereas the Transformer accepts greater churn and repair penalty to accumulate more return. A mission that prioritizes command stability, operator predictability, or limited replanning authority should encode those requirements directly, for example through stronger eviction costs or explicit constrained objectives. We did not perform a reward-weight sensitivity sweep, so the architecture ranking should be interpreted for the reported objective rather than as invariant to all operational preferences.

The computational profile in Table 2 suggests that the hybrid loop is lightweight on the training host. The Transformer contains about 0.58 million trainable parameters; its mean policy-inference and environment-step timers are 1.81 ms and 4.31 ms, respectively, with the latter already including repair, resource updates, and the next observation. These measurements are encouraging for on-board use but are not flight-processor benchmarks; Orekit-rail preparation and hardware-specific qualification remain separate engineering tasks.

The unchanged warm-start plan was not scored as a separate baseline. This limits the claims that can be made about improvement over a frozen ground schedule, but it does not weaken the controlled question addressed here: which policy architecture best selects incremental edits when the initial scenario and deterministic repair layer are held fixed. The 1000 paired test episodes, together with the feasibility, downlink, and repair diagnostics in Tables 3 and 4 and Figure 3, provide direct evidence for that comparison.

The single-satellite scope is likewise a limitation of the present evaluation rather than an architectural dead end. In a constellation, the same local policy–repair loop could run on each spacecraft while a coordination layer exchanges already committed observations, remaining requests, shared ground-station reservations, and time-stamped resource summaries. Those updates could repopulate each satellite’s candidate bank and global state without moving hard local feasibility checks out of the repair layer. For homogeneous platforms using the same normalized interface, a common policy could in principle be deployed on each satellite; heterogeneous dynamics or action semantics would likely require adaptation or retraining. This distributed extension has not been evaluated, and communication delay, duplicate observations, and cross-platform conflicts still require an explicit coordination protocol.

Cross-mission transfer and reward sensitivity also remain open. Unseen targets can enter the existing candidate interface, but different spacecraft dynamics, constraint semantics, or action types may require retraining. Moreover, no reward-weight sensitivity sweep was performed, so the reported architecture ranking applies to the stated operational objective. These limitations define the next evaluation steps while preserving the central result: typed candidate-wise attention improves the learned decision component of the hybrid scheduler under the tested conditions.
